h1: Fix & Flip Renovations Built Around the Deal
lede: Every day a flip sits unfinished, money is lost. Genstone Construction plans and runs fix-and-flip renovations around the numbers that decide your profit: the purchase price, the after-repair value, the carrying cost and the date the house hits the market. We put renovation dollars into the improvements buyers pay for, keep a close eye on budget and schedule, and hand you a house that is ready to list and ready to survive a buyer's inspection.

sections.h2: Why the calendar matters as much as the budget
sections.body:
On a flip, time is a line item even though it never shows up on the contractor's estimate. Every day between closing and the resale closing, you are paying interest or giving up return on your own cash, plus property taxes, insurance on a vacant house, utilities and the occasional lawn cut or snow removal. A rehab that comes in on budget but runs long can quietly eat the margin you underwrote.

That is why we treat the schedule as part of the scope rather than something that falls out of it. Before work starts, you get a construction schedule with anticipated milestones, and your field manager reviews it with you. The sequencing is built so trades are not waiting on each other: demolition and debris removal first, then the rough-in work that needs inspection, then the inspections themselves, then drywall, cabinets, flooring, paint and trim, and finally the punch list and cleaning.

The common schedule killers on investor rehabs are predictable. Materials with long lead times get ordered after demo instead of before it. A permit is pulled late, so the rough-in sits waiting for an inspector. A change of mind on finishes halfway through sends a trade back to redo work. Our front-end scoping is designed to catch these before anyone swings a hammer, so long-lead items are identified early, permits are applied for as soon as the scope is settled, and finish selections are locked before they hold anyone up.

None of this means rushing. A house that lists with sloppy trim, uneven tile or an unpermitted panel swap tends to sit, collect lowball offers or fall out of contract. The goal is a steady pace with no dead days, not a sprint that creates rework.

sections.h2: Put renovation dollars where buyers actually notice them
sections.body:
Successful flips need more than construction skill. They need a renovation strategy that starts with the comps. If the renovated sales in the neighborhood have quartz counters, luxury vinyl plank and a painted brick fireplace, that is the bar. Going well above it rarely gets paid back, and falling below it shows up immediately in buyer feedback and offer prices.

We help you prioritize the improvements that move buyer appeal and marketability without overspending on upgrades the property or the market will not support. In practice the money usually concentrates in a few places:

- The kitchen, because it carries the listing photos and sets the buyer's impression of the whole house.
- Bathrooms, especially the primary bath, where dated tile and fixtures read as a project the buyer will have to take on.
- Flooring and paint throughout, which make a house feel finished for a relatively modest share of the budget.
- Curb appeal: the front door, lighting, landscaping cleanup, gutters and anything that makes the first photo look cared for.
- Lighting and hardware, which are inexpensive and change how every room photographs.

Where we push back is on spending that does not show up in the sale price. An oversized addition in a neighborhood of small ranches, a high-end appliance package on a starter home, or custom tile work that a buyer in that price range will not pay for are common examples. Sometimes the right call is to keep a solid original feature, such as hardwood that only needs refinishing, rather than tearing it out.

Every scope we write is matched to the property's likely buyer, not to a generic idea of a renovated house.

sections.h2: Plan for the buyer's inspection before you list
sections.body:
A buyer's home inspector is the second appraisal of your work, and plenty of flips that looked great in photos lose money during the inspection period. The issues that trigger renegotiation are rarely cosmetic. They are the roof that has a few years left, an electrical panel with a known problem brand or double-tapped breakers, missing GFCI protection in the kitchen and baths, an old water heater, galvanized supply lines, a cast-iron drain with a belly in it, poor grading that sends water toward the foundation, or a furnace nobody has serviced in a decade.

We would rather address those in the scope than watch you hand back credit at the closing table. During the Pre-Offer Rehab Review and the site walk that follows, our estimators look past the finishes to the systems a buyer's inspector will test. That does not mean every flip gets a new roof and new mechanicals. It means you know which items are likely to come up, what they cost to correct, and whether correcting them now is cheaper than negotiating them later.

Permits are part of the same thinking. Buyers, their agents and their lenders increasingly ask whether major work was permitted, and unpermitted electrical, plumbing, structural or HVAC work can stall a sale or force a price cut. Our team coordinates required permits and inspections as part of project management, and the documentation is kept organized so you can hand it to the buyer's side when asked.

A clean inspection report is one of the most reliable ways to protect your sale price and keep a contract on schedule.

sections.h2: Scopes, estimates and multiple ARV plans
sections.body:
A vague bid is how flips go over budget. Before work begins, you receive a detailed scope document and estimate that lists the anticipated labor and material costs line by line, along with the project's draw schedule. Dumpster and debris removal costs are included in the estimate, so they do not appear later as a surprise.

Where it helps the decision, we develop more than one renovation plan for the same house. Each plan pairs a finish level and scope with the after-repair value it is designed to support. A typical set might include:

- A lighter plan that fixes what a buyer's inspection would flag and refreshes paint, floors and fixtures, aimed at a quick sale to a value-minded buyer.
- A mid-level plan that renovates the kitchen and baths to match the bulk of the renovated comps.
- A fuller plan that reconfigures layout, opens a wall or adds a bathroom where the comps show buyers paying for it.

Seeing the plans side by side lets you compare the added cost of each step against the added resale value and the extra time it takes. Sometimes the fuller plan clearly wins. Sometimes the extra months of carrying cost and the risk of a thinner buyer pool at the higher price make the middle plan the smarter bet. The numbers are yours to weigh, and we lay them out plainly so you can.

Scopes also protect you during the job. When the scope is specific about materials, quantities and locations, there is far less room for disagreement about what was included, and change orders become rare rather than routine.

sections.h2: How a Genstone flip runs from closing to listing
sections.body:
Every project has a designated field manager who stays with it from start to finish. That person is your primary point of contact, oversees the local crews, maintains our quality standards and deals with problems as they come up. You are not passed between departments or left chasing a subcontractor for updates.

Genstone operates with national scale and local execution. We coordinate vetted, licensed and insured local contractors in your market from a network of thousands, and we verify that the contractors assigned to your project carry appropriate insurance and meet applicable licensing requirements. Our estimators, field managers, repair specialists and billing team each handle their part of the process, which keeps scoping, field work and payment from bottlenecking on one person.

You can follow progress, documentation and project milestones without driving to the property. That matters when you are working several deals at once, investing out of state, or simply do not want to spend your afternoons on a jobsite.

When something unexpected turns up behind a wall or under a floor, the process is the same every time. The field manager documents the condition, we review the cost and schedule impact with you, and nothing proceeds until you approve the change in writing. Thorough front-end scoping is designed to keep those moments uncommon.

At the end, the field manager walks the house, the punch list is closed, the site is cleaned, and the final billing is issued only after completion and your approval. The work carries a one-year workmanship warranty.

sections.h2: Draws, lenders and the rest of the capital stack
sections.body:
No upfront payment is required. Construction draws are tied to completed work, and final payment is due after the project is finished and you have approved it. That structure keeps your cash working on the acquisition instead of sitting with a contractor, and it aligns with how most fix-and-flip lenders release rehab funds.

If your rehab is financed, the draw schedule in your estimate can be organized around your lender's draw inspections, so each request lines up with work the inspector can see and verify. Lien waivers are collected as part of our risk-management process, which keeps the title clean when you sell and gives your lender the paper trail it expects.

Because Genstone Construction is part of the Genstone Companies, the rest of the flip can stay under one roof if you want it to. Genstone Financial offers fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit. Genstone Insurance writes coverage for fix-and-flip and vacant properties. Title Clearing & Escrow handles title and settlement on the purchase and the sale. Genstone Realty can help with acquisition and with listing the finished house. None of it is required to hire us, but having the lender, the contractor and the title company working from the same scope and schedule removes a lot of friction.

If the market shifts mid-project and holding the house as a rental starts to make more sense than selling, the same team can adjust the finish plan toward rental durability and connect you with Genstone Financial's DSCR rental loans and Genstone Property Management.

sections.h2: Two ways to start: before you offer or after you close
sections.body:
If you are still evaluating a property, start with a complimentary Pre-Offer Rehab Review. Send the address, the listing or your photos, and what you are thinking of paying. Our team estimates the anticipated renovation costs, helps refine the after-repair value, and tells you whether the repairs and projected resale economics support the offer you are considering. It is the cheapest way to avoid buying a house whose rehab cannot be paid back.

The review is most useful early, while you can still adjust your price, ask for a repair credit or walk away. Investors also use it to compare two or three candidate properties and put their offer behind the one with the cleanest rehab math.

If you already own the property, send us your project details, including photos, and we will help you develop the renovation scope. Useful items to include are any inspection report you have, the comps you used to set your resale target, your budget and your lender's draw requirements. From there we schedule a site walk, build the detailed scope and estimate, and assign your field manager.

We work on single-family homes and small multifamily properties of two to four units, and the same discipline applies to both. On a small multifamily flip the buyer pool may include owner-occupants using FHA financing or investors underwriting on rent, and the scope should reflect who is most likely to buy.

Call (312) 429-2637 or send your property through the Pre-Offer Rehab Review form to get started.

faqs.q: Do you only work on single-family flips?
faqs.a: No. Most of our fix-and-flip work is single-family, but we also renovate small multifamily properties of two to four units for resale. The approach is the same: match the scope to the likely buyer and the renovated comps, control the schedule, and fix what an inspection would flag. On a two-to-four unit property, the likely buyer may be an owner-occupant or an investor underwriting on rents, and that changes which improvements are worth paying for.

faqs.q: How do you decide which improvements are worth doing?
faqs.a: We start with the comps and the likely buyer. Renovated sales nearby set the finish level buyers expect at your target price. From there we prioritize the kitchen, baths, flooring, paint, curb appeal and any system a buyer's inspector would flag, and we push back on upgrades the market will not pay for. When the right answer is unclear, we price multiple ARV plans so you can compare added cost against added resale value.

faqs.q: Can I get an estimate before I buy the house?
faqs.a: Yes. The complimentary Pre-Offer Rehab Review is built for that moment. Send us the address, photos or listing and your intended offer, and we estimate anticipated renovation costs, help refine the after-repair value and tell you whether the repairs and projected resale economics support the price. Many investors use it to negotiate, and some use it to decide not to buy.

faqs.q: How does payment work on a flip?
faqs.a: There is no upfront payment. Construction draws are tied to completed work, and the final payment is due after the project is complete and you have approved it. If your rehab is financed, we can organize the draw schedule around your lender's draw inspections so each request matches work the inspector can verify. Lien waivers are collected along the way.

faqs.q: What happens if you find something unexpected during demolition?
faqs.a: Your field manager documents the condition with photos and a description, and we review the cost and schedule impact with you before anything proceeds. Approved changes are written into the scope. Detailed front-end scoping, including a close look at the systems behind the finishes, is designed to keep these moments uncommon, but older houses do sometimes hide rot, failed plumbing or prior unpermitted work.

faqs.q: Will I have a timeline before work begins?
faqs.a: Yes. Every project includes a construction schedule with anticipated milestones and timing, which we review with you before work starts. Your field manager keeps you informed as the job moves, and you can follow progress and documentation without visiting the site. On a flip, the schedule is treated as part of the scope because carrying cost is part of your return.

faqs.q: Can Genstone help with financing and selling the finished house?
faqs.a: Genstone Construction is part of the Genstone Companies. Genstone Financial offers fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit, Genstone Insurance covers fix-and-flip and vacant properties, Title Clearing & Escrow handles closings, and Genstone Realty supports acquisition and disposition. You can use any of them or none, and many investors start with just one. Hiring us for the renovation does not require using the other companies.
